prompt: What is the basic difference between a framework like Django and a library like requests?
hint: Who calls whom?

choices.text: A framework is larger and includes more functions to call
choices.why: Size is not the difference; a big library is still something you call.

choices.text: The framework calls your functions
choices.why: Right. It owns the request loop and runs your code when a route matches.

choices.text: A library runs in its own process
choices.why: Both run inside your Python process.

choices.text: Only a framework can make HTTP requests
choices.why: requests makes HTTP requests; a framework answers them.

prompt: Match each job a web application needs to an example of it.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: an age that is not a number is refused
a session cookie says who is asking
an attendee may not delete an event

right_distractors: the page is served from a cache

prompt: An event has 40 seats. Which part of the work can the framework NOT know without you?
hint: The framework knows types, not your rules.

choices.text: That capacity has to be a positive integer
choices.why: That is a type rule, and a framework checks it if you declare it.

choices.text: Which function answers /events/
choices.why: Routing is the framework's job once you declare the route.

choices.text: That the 41st registration is refused
choices.why: Right. That is a rule of your domain, and lesson 4 makes the database enforce it.

prompt: Django was born at a newspaper. Which of its assumptions comes most directly from that?
hint: Staff edited content on deadlines.

choices.text: Staff need a back office to edit the data
choices.why: Right. The admin exists because editors had to change rows without a developer.

choices.text: Requests spend most of their time waiting on other services
choices.why: That is FastAPI's assumption, and async is its answer.

choices.text: Type hints are the specification of the API
choices.why: That is FastAPI's; Django predates type hints in Python.

choices.text: The response is JSON for a mobile app
choices.why: Django's first job was HTML pages.

prompt: Match each part of the job to how FastAPI handles it.
hint: The side-by-side table.

prompt: FastAPI has no ORM, no admin and no login in the box. What does that mean for a team?
hint: Read the empty cells.

choices.text: Those parts are not needed in an API
choices.why: An API with users still needs logins and data; somebody provides them.

choices.text: The team chooses and maintains each one
choices.why: Right. An empty cell is a decision and a version to maintain.

choices.text: FastAPI generates them from the type hints
choices.why: It generates validation and a schema, not a database layer or logins.

choices.text: The application will run faster than a Django one
choices.why: Missing features do not make the remaining code faster.

prompt: Where does Flask sit between the two?
hint: Its core, and its style of call.

choices.text: It is Django without the ORM
choices.why: Flask was never part of Django.

choices.text: An async framework built on Starlette, like FastAPI but smaller
choices.why: That describes FastAPI.

choices.text: A small core like FastAPI's, synchronous like classic Django
choices.why: Right, extended with plug-ins.

choices.text: A server that runs Django and FastAPI applications
choices.why: Gunicorn and Uvicorn are servers; Flask is a framework.

prompt: Why does this course recommend a virtual machine more firmly than the python course did?
hint: What gets installed from lesson 4 on?

choices.text: PostgreSQL, Redis, nginx and Docker run as services started at boot
choices.why: Right. On a machine you also work on they collide with what is already there.

choices.text: Django refuses to run outside Linux
choices.why: Django runs on macOS and Windows too.

choices.text: uv cannot be installed on macOS
choices.why: uv has installers for every system.

choices.text: Python 3.12 is not available on macOS or Windows any other way
choices.why: python.org publishes it for every system.

prompt: Put the setup steps in order, on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04.
hint: pipx comes from apt; uv comes from pipx.
items: sudo apt install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip pipx git curl
trap: Checking uv before opening a new terminal answers 'command not found', because the old terminal read its PATH when it opened.

prompt: Right after pipx ensurepath, the same terminal says uv: command not found. What fixes it?
hint: When does a terminal read PATH?

choices.text: Run pipx install uv again
choices.why: uv is installed; the terminal does not know where to look yet.

choices.text: Open a new terminal
choices.why: Right, or source ~/.bashrc in this one.

choices.text: Install uv with apt instead
choices.why: Ubuntu 24.04 does not package uv, and the PATH is the problem.

choices.text: Reboot the virtual machine and reinstall Python
choices.why: A new terminal is enough, and nothing is wrong with Python.

prompt: python3 manage.py check says Couldn't import Django, and uv add django succeeded a minute ago. Why?
hint: Which Python is python3?

choices.text: Django 6.1 does not support Python 3.12
choices.why: It does; 3.12 is the oldest it supports.

choices.text: uv add only edits pyproject.toml and installs nothing
choices.why: It installed three packages into .venv.

choices.text: python3 is the system's Python; Django is in .venv
choices.why: Right. uv run python manage.py check runs it inside the environment.

choices.text: manage.py has to be made executable first
choices.why: Permissions would give a different error, and python3 file.py needs none.

prompt: runserver stops with That port is already in use. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Only one program can listen on a port.

choices.text: Another user's Django project on the same machine
choices.why: Possible on a shared machine, but on yours it is your own server.

choices.text: A server you started earlier is still running
choices.why: Right. Find its terminal and press Ctrl-C.

choices.text: The 18 unapplied migrations
choices.why: That warning is printed before the error and is unrelated to the port.

choices.text: Port 8000 is reserved for root
choices.why: Only ports below 1024 need root.

prompt: How many packages did uv install for the FastAPI project?
hint: Count the + lines, or read the comparison.

prompt: Which headers did Django add to the hello response without being asked? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of them, from middleware.

choices.text: X-Frame-Options: DENY
choices.why: Right. A browser will not show the page inside another site's frame.

choices.text: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
choices.why: Right. The browser trusts the declared type instead of guessing.

choices.text: server: uvicorn
choices.why: That is uvicorn's own header on the FastAPI answer.

choices.text: Referrer-Policy: same-origin
choices.why: Right. Links to other sites do not reveal the page they came from.

choices.text: Transfer-Encoding: chunked
choices.why: That was the bare ASGI application, which sent no length.

prompt: Why did the FastAPI project need uvicorn as well as fastapi?
hint: What listens on the port?

choices.text: It listens on the port
choices.why: Right. FastAPI is not a server; Django's runserver does both jobs in one command.

choices.text: uvicorn converts the dictionary to JSON
choices.why: FastAPI does that; uvicorn sends the bytes.

choices.text: uvicorn generates the /openapi.json document
choices.why: FastAPI generates it from the routes.

choices.text: FastAPI cannot read path parameters without it
choices.why: Path parameters are FastAPI's routing.

prompt: The hello endpoint uses no database, yet Django warned about 18 unapplied migrations. What does that show?
hint: Whose tables are they?

choices.text: That uv installed Django twice
choices.why: One Django is installed; the warning is about tables.

choices.text: That the endpoint will fail until they are applied
choices.why: It answered 200 with the migrations pending.

choices.text: That its built-in apps want tables, used or not
choices.why: Right. Users, sessions and the admin all want tables.

prompt: In WSGI, how does the application hand the body back to the server?
hint: Look at the last line of the function.

choices.text: By awaiting send with a body message
choices.why: That is ASGI.

choices.text: As the return value of the call
choices.why: Right. start_response carries the status and headers, the return value the body.

choices.text: By writing to a file the server reads
choices.why: Nothing is written to disk.

choices.text: Through a callback named receive
choices.why: receive belongs to ASGI, and it brings data in.

prompt: A WSGI server has 8 workers, and every request waits 2 seconds on another service. What limits it?
hint: What does a worker do while the call blocks?

choices.text: At most 8 such requests are answered at a time
choices.why: Right. Each worker is held for the whole wait.

choices.text: The CPU, which is busy for the whole 2 seconds of each request
choices.why: The CPU is idle while the worker waits.

choices.text: Nothing, because WSGI awaits the service
choices.why: WSGI is synchronous; there is no await.

choices.text: The size of the response bodies
choices.why: The wait, not the body, holds the worker.

prompt: Django's runserver answered with the header Server: ___/0.2, which is the standard library's WSGI server.
hint: The same name appears on the bare WSGI app's answer.

prompt: A team fluent in Django must ship a small JSON API next month. What does the lesson suggest weighs most?
hint: The cheapest expertise there is.

choices.text: FastAPI's benchmarks, since the API is small
choices.why: Most request time goes to the database, not the framework.

choices.text: Whichever framework is newer
choices.why: Newness is not a reason that stays true in a year.

choices.text: What the team already knows
choices.why: Right. The table says either fits a JSON API, and knowledge tips it.

choices.text: Flask, because it sits in the middle
choices.why: Choosing a third framework adds a second set of answers to maintain.

prompt: When is FastAPI faster in a way users notice?
hint: Waiting, not computing.

choices.text: When a request runs a slow database query
choices.why: A slow query is equally slow under both.

choices.text: When the response is a large JSON body
choices.why: Serialising is not where the difference lies.

choices.text: When many requests wait on slow services at the same time
choices.why: Right. ASGI lets the server serve others during the wait; lesson 9 measures it.

choices.text: When the code computes a large report
choices.why: Computing holds the process whatever the framework.

prompt: A colleague says: 'FastAPI is better because it has fewer dependencies.' The comparison showed 14 packages against Django's 3. What is wrong with the claim?
hint: Count, and then ask what is missing.

choices.text: Nothing: 14 is fewer than Django's 47 MB
choices.why: Packages and megabytes are different units.

choices.text: Its count was higher, and parts are still missing
choices.why: Right. A database layer and a password hasher arrive in lessons 10 and 11.

choices.text: Django's three packages are written in C
choices.why: Django is pure Python; that is not the point.

choices.text: uv counts optional packages twice
choices.why: uv pip list counts each installed package once.
